newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Shelling halts aid distribution in Zaire's Goma.
newsitem.headline: Shelling halts aid distribution in Zaire's Goma.

text.p: Four shells slammed into a hill in the eastern Zairean city of Goma on Wednesday, prompting U.N. officials to suspend distribution of aid, a U.N. spokesman said.

Damien Persannaz, a spokesman for the U.N. Children's Fund, said U.N. trucks sent to Goma Central Hospital to deliver aid were ordered to pull back to the U.N. refugee agency compound because of the shelling.
Some of 10 tonnes of food aid had been unloaded at the hospital before the halt was ordered by U.N. officials.
The food, medical supplies and some blankets arrived in Goma from Rwanda on Monday but distribution had been delayed until Wednesday by talks between rebels and aid agency officials.
The shelling erupted after rebels fired at an unidentified plane which made at least three passes over the eastern city.
A total of four mortar bombs or artillery rounds slammed into the foot of Mount Goma shortly after rebels fired towards Mugunga refugee camp to the west from Mount Goma, witnesses said.
It was not immediately known if there were any casualties.
Rebel gunners had fired at a twin-propeller light plane flying repeatedly over Goma, saying they suspected it was carrying French troops, but it was not apparently hit.

The 10 tonnes of food, some medical supplies and blankets were taken to the hospital following an agreement between rebel leader Laurent Kabila and U.N. officials on aid operations in rebel territory.
"This is enough food to feed 2,500 people for 14 days," said Francis Mwanza, a spokesman for the U.N. World Food Programme.
The aid which was brought in by U.N. and independent agencies had been kept at the city's main football stadium under rebel guard before both sides agreed on how to distribute it.
Mwanza said a total of 750 tonnes of food were in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi and 150 tonnes of it was maize already loaded on trucks and ready to move across into Goma city.
Aid workers said the arrival of more food and supplies depended on talks with the rebels and the security situation.

UNICEF's Persannaz said it was very hard to assess the need for a massive aid operation in the area because there was very little information about the situation in Mugunga, which was the world's largest refugee camp with some 400,000 residents.
Rebel forces say Mugunga is held by exiled Rwandan troops and militiamen who were responsible for Rwanda's 1994 genocide and are using the refugees as "human shields" against an attack.
